title: Yesterday
goal: Talk about what has already happened — one inserted letter turns the whole sentence into the past, and the negative uses a completely different form.
bekal: insert **-i-** to form the past tense
negate the past with the *-nut/-nyt* and *-neet* forms
tell a story from beginning to end

dialogs.title: Dialog — Viikonloppu mökillä
dialogs.intro: Monday morning. Budi finally went along to the cottage last weekend, and Aino wants to hear all about it.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: No niin! Mitä te teitte viikonloppuna?
lines.id: Well then! What did you guys do at the weekend?
lines.literal: well so! what you(pl) did at-weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Me lähdimme perjantaina. Ajoimme kaksi tuntia autolla.
lines.id: We left on Friday. We drove for two hours.
lines.literal: we left on-Friday. drove-we two hour-part by-car.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Se oli pieni ja vanha. Ei ollut suihkua eikä nettiä.
lines.id: It was small and old. No shower and no internet.
lines.literal: it was small and old. not been shower-part and-not internet-part.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Se on koko idea! Menitkö saunaan?
lines.id: That's the whole idea! Did you go in the sauna?
lines.literal: it is whole idea! went-?-you into-sauna?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Menin. Marek lämmitti saunan, ja me istuimme siellä tunnin.
lines.id: I did. Marek heated the sauna, and we sat there for an hour.
lines.literal: went-I. Marek heated sauna-whole, and we sat there hour-whole.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.id: Did you swim in the lake afterwards?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En uinut. Katsoin vain. Vesi oli neljä astetta!
lines.id: No. I just watched. The water was four degrees!
lines.literal: not-I swum. watched-I only. water was four degree-part!

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Ha! Ensi kerralla. Mitä te söitte?
lines.id: Ha! Next time. What did you eat?
lines.literal: ha! next on-time. what you(pl) ate?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Grillasimme makkaraa ja joimme olutta. Marek lauloi.
lines.id: We grilled sausages and drank beer. Marek sang.
lines.literal: grilled-we sausage-part and drank-we beer-part. Marek sang.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Sinä et kertonut, että Marek laulaa.
lines.id: You never told me Marek sings.
lines.literal: you not told, that Marek sings.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En tiennyt itsekään. Emme nukkuneet paljon.
lines.id: I didn't know either. We didn't sleep much.
lines.literal: not-I known self-either. not-we slept much.

notes: **One letter changes the whole tense.** *Menen* (I go) → *men**i**n* (I went). The inserted *-i-* sits between the stem and the personal ending, and the ending doesn't change at all. Compare English, where *go → went* can change the whole word; Finnish is far more regular.

**The hän form loses its ending.** *Hän menee* → *hän meni*; *hän lukee* → *hän luki*. The long vowel of the present is replaced by *-i*, so the past *hän* form is actually shorter. This is the most reliable sign of the past tense in a text.
**Oli, not olei.** *Olla* in the past: *olin, olit, oli, olimme, olitte, olivat*. These forms appear in almost every story, so learn them now, before anything else.

**The negative uses a completely different form.** *En uinut*, *en tiennyt*, *emme nukkuneet*. The negative verb is still *en/et/ei/emme/ette/eivät* — what changes is the main verb, which takes *-nut/-nyt* (one person) or *-neet* (several people). The inserted *-i-* disappears completely in the negative.
**Eikä nettiä** — "and no internet". Once again *-kä* links two negatives, as you learned in unit 7.

**Söitte from syödä.** Some verbs change their vowel as well: *syödä → söin*, *juoda → join*, *tehdä → tein*, *nähdä → näin*, *tietää → tiesin*. The list is short but very frequent; it's in this unit's reference table.

grammars.title: The past tense — inserting -i-
body: Finnish has only one simple past tense, formed by inserting **-i-** between the stem and the personal ending. The endings are exactly the ones you already know.
after: **Stems ending in -u, -o, -y, -ö: just add the -i-.** *Asun → asuin*, *sanon → sanoin*, *katson → katsoin*. The easiest and largest group.

⚠️ **Stems ending in -a/-ä: the vowel disappears or changes.** If the first syllable has *o* or *u*, the final vowel **disappears**: *ostan → ostin*, *muistan → muistin*. If the first syllable has *a* or *e*, the final vowel becomes **-o-**: *annan → annoin*, *maksan → maksoin*, *alan → aloin*.
**Stems ending in -e: the -e disappears.** *Tulen → tulin*, *menen → menin*, *nousen → nousin*, *opiskelen → opiskelin*.

grammars.title: Negating the past
body: The form is completely different from the positive sentence, and this is what needs the most practice in this unit. The negative verb stays the same; the main verb changes its clothes.
after: **The rule fits in two lines:** one person takes **-nut/-nyt**, several people take **-neet**. Choose *u* or *y* by vowel harmony: *nukkunut* but *mennyt*.
How to form it: take the stem of the dictionary form and add the ending. *Puhua → puhu**nut***, *asua → asu**nut***, *ostaa → osta**nut***, *lukea → luke**nut***.

⚠️ Type 3 verbs double their consonant: *tulla → tul**lut***, *mennä → men**nyt***, *nousta → nous**sut***, *opiskella → opiskel**lut***. The pattern: the stem's last consonant takes the place of the *n*.

sections.title: Past-tense verbs to learn by heart

blocks.text: These verbs change more than just adding *-i-*. The list is short, but all of them are very frequent — they cover most everyday stories.

⚠️ Notice the *t → s* pattern in *tietää → tiesin* and *ymmärtää → ymmärsin*. It applies to several verbs ending in *-ta/-tä*: *pyytää → pyysin* (ask for), *löytää → löysin* (find), *huutaa → huusin* (shout).

*Koska* has two jobs: "because" and "when". Only its position tells them apart — at the start of a question it means "when" (*Koska tulit?*), in the middle of a sentence "because" (*En tullut, koska olin kipeä*).

blocks.title: The practice that pays off most at this stage
items: Every evening, write **three sentences** about your day in the past tense. One positive, one negative, one question.
*Menin kauppaan. En ostanut mitään. Miksi kävin siellä?*
Three sentences a day for a month makes ninety sentences — far more than you'd get from reading the tables over and over.
What did you guys do at the weekend?
The cottage was small and old.

answers: Minä menin kauppaan. — Sinä olit kotona. — Hän luki kirjaa. — Me ostimme leipää. — Te tulitte myöhään. — He asuivat Helsingissä.
En mennyt saunaan. — En uinut järvessä. — Hän ei nukkunut hyvin. — Me emme olleet mökillä. — Te ette syöneet makkaraa. — He eivät tulleet perjantaina.
